memoryText: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Job 42:5 slowly, several times, then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or discuss.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Job 42:5 is the center of the book of Job. After forty-one chapters of arguing, questioning, suffering, and listening, Job says something quiet.

“I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear.” This is how most of us begin. We hear about God from our parents, a preacher, a book, or a friend. We know the facts. We can say the creeds. That is a good beginning, and it is a real knowledge, but it is secondhand. It is a report.

“But now my eye sees you.” Something has changed. Job has encountered God. He is no longer relying on what others have said. He has seen the Lord in the whirlwind, heard his voice, and been met by his presence. The word “now” tells you that this is the result of everything that has come before. Suffering, with all its pain, led him here.

This is one of the most hopeful statements in the Bible. It means that the purpose of suffering, in the deepest sense, is not to teach us a lesson or to punish us. It is to bring us to the place where we see God. This does not mean that the suffering is good in itself. It is not. But God can use it to give you a clearer sight of himself than you had before.

For the Christian, the verse is even richer. In Jesus, “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). He is the one in whom the invisible God has become visible. To see Jesus is to see the Father (John 14:9). Every Christian’s journey is from hearing to seeing, and it is finished when we see him face to face.
weekInReview: This week you finished the book of Job. You read God’s answer from the whirlwind and the questions about creation that silenced Job. You read the last chapters, in which God vindicated Job over his friends, Job prayed for them, and the LORD restored his fortunes. You paused for two doctrinal days: on the decrees of God and providence, and on suffering and the Christian life. You saw that God rules over every event, that he is not the author of sin, and that Christians suffer in union with a suffering Savior. You prayed three psalms alongside Job. Psalm 73 showed you the sanctuary as the place where perspective returns. Psalm 88 gave you a prayer for the dark that has no easy ending. Psalm 17 gave you the hope of seeing God’s face. The week taught that the answer to suffering is the presence of God.
reflectionQuestions: Job went from hearing about God to seeing him. Where are you on that path? What would it look like for your knowledge of God to become less secondhand?

How does Jesus, the visible image of the invisible God, fulfill what Job longed for? Think about a moment in the Gospels where Jesus shows you what God is like, and what it means that you can see him there.
Of the three psalms you read this week, which one was closest to where you are right now? Write a prayer in your own words that begins with that psalm.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to see him and not only hear of him.
Thank him for Jesus, in whom you see his glory.
Ask him to use suffering to draw you nearer.
